narrowest_regime: Holds whenever the shown RMSE is sqrt of the pooled out-of-fold MSE for each family on the same rows (and same folds/repeats); it would fail only if 'RMSE' were the mean of per-fold RMSEs, which is not what the claim says.
reason: Pooled RMSE = sqrt(pooled MSE) and sqrt is strictly increasing on [0, inf), so the ordering of families (and ties) is identical under either score. Only the arithmetic of differences/ratios changes (e.g., a 10% MSE gain is ~5% in RMSE), not which family is lower. Averaging per-fold RMSEs instead would break the equivalence by Jensen's inequality, but that is not the pooled score described.
bite_note: Ranking is invariant, so the family the researcher picks cannot change; only the displayed magnitudes of gaps differ.

failing_part: "give the same nutrient effect for any functional form" / "a restricted cubic spline of the energy residual estimates the nutrient's substitution curve ... exactly as a spline of the nutrient with energy beside it does"
narrowest_regime: Equivalence holds only for a nutrient term that is linear (residual r = N - a - bE is an affine function of N and E, so b*r + cE reparameterizes b*N + c'E), or trivially when the nutrient is uncorrelated with energy in the sample (b = 0).
reason: For a nonlinear f, f(N - a - bE) + cE is not of the form g(N) + dE: at fixed energy the residual-spline curve is the same shape shifted along N by bE, so its implied substitution curve changes with the energy level. In a simulation (n = 20,000, corr(N,E) = 0.63, true curve -0.002(N-60)^2 at fixed E), the nutrient spline + E recovered the curve at every energy level (dy for N 45->60 ~0.40 vs true 0.45), while the residual spline + E gave -0.18, 0.41 and 1.22 at E = 1600, 2000, 2400 and had R^2 0.25 vs 0.56. Willett, Howe & Kushi state the residual/standard equivalence for linear models; the citation does not support extending it to splines.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S

bite_note: For a curved exposure correlated with energy, recommending the residual spline yields a different (and energy-dependent) dose-response curve than the substitution curve the researcher asked for; the natural alternative (spline of the nutrient plus energy) gives the right answer.

failing_part: "no finite estimate exists, so the standardized risk difference and ratio are refused"
narrowest_regime: Only the coefficient for the separated group diverges. The standardized risk ratio fails to be finite only when one arm's standardized risk is exactly 0 (e.g., zero events in the control arm across all strata); the standardized risk difference is always finite (it lies in [-1, 1]).
reason: Under separation the MLE of the separated coefficient diverges, but the fitted probabilities converge, to 0 or 1 for the separated group, which is that group's observed risk. So g-computation risks, and the RD and RR built from them, have finite limits. In a simulated trial where a covariate stratum had 100% events, the stratum coefficient grew without bound (7.3 -> 19.0 as the penalty went to 0) while the standardized RD (-0.1258) and RR (0.649) stayed fixed and matched saturated stratum standardization (-0.1258). Inference is harder (Wald intervals for the coefficient fail), but Firth penalization, profile or exact intervals, or collapsing the stratum all handle it; refusing on the grounds that no finite estimate exists is wrong.

citations.cite: Albert A, Anderson JA. On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika 1984;71:1-10
Heinze G, Schemper M. A solution to the problem of separation in logistic regression. Stat Med 2002;21:2409-2419

bite_note: Separation in a small covariate stratum is common in trials with rare or near-universal events. The refusal withholds the primary trial effect when a finite, estimable RD (and usually RR) exists.

failing_part: "the CR1 sandwich ... with a G/(G-1) correction and a t(G-1) reference gives valid 95% intervals"
narrowest_regime: Approximately valid (coverage about 94%) when there are many units of similar size, and asymptotically valid as G grows. Wald intervals from the inverse observed information are asymptotically valid for independent rows without sparse categories or separation.
reason: The cited source supports t(G-1) as a minimum, not as sufficient. Cameron & Miller write 'at a minimum one should use the T(G-1) distribution rather than the standard normal', say the G/(G-1) factor 'usually lessens, but does not fully eliminate' the CRVE's downward bias, report over-rejection even with T(G-1) critical values, especially for unbalanced clusters, and recommend bias-adjusted (CR2/Bell-McCaffrey) SEs or a wild cluster bootstrap for few clusters. In a simulation of a clustered logit (the 2-category proportional-odds case) with a unit-level covariate, CR1 + t(G-1) covered about 94% with balanced units (G = 10/20/50), but 85.5%, 88% and 88% with lognormal unit sizes at G = 10/20/50. The 'unit floor' is unspecified, so it cannot be credited with rescuing validity.

citations.cite: Cameron AC, Miller DL. A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference. J Human Resources 2015;50(2):317-372 (quote checked in text, §VI)
MacKinnon JG, Webb MD. Wild bootstrap inference for wildly different cluster sizes. J Appl Econometrics 2017;32:233-254 (working paper 2013)
Bell RM, McCaffrey DF. Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Survey Methodology 2002

bite_note: With few or very unequal units (e.g., 10-30 sites of differing size), the reported 95% intervals undercover by 5-10 points. A CR2/Satterthwaite or wild-cluster-bootstrap interval would be wider and could change significance calls on the ordinal coefficient table.

failing_part: "intervals that treat the PSUs as unstratified, which are too narrow where people were sampled in clusters"
narrowest_regime: Intervals come out too narrow only when PSU codes are reused within strata (e.g., NHANES-style PSU 1/2 in every stratum), so that dropping strata merges different PSUs into a few pseudo-clusters, and a normal reference is used. Blocking until the user attests is a defensible guard against that coding hazard.
reason: The PSU column already captures the clustering. Dropping stratification from a with-replacement linearization adds the between-stratum variation, so with uniquely coded PSUs the variance is usually overestimated (conservative), not too narrow. In a simulation of 15 strata x 2 PSUs, unique PSU codes gave unstratified interval widths 1.0-1.8x the stratified ones, with coverage 95-100% against 95%. Only reused PSU codes with a z reference gave narrow intervals (about 70% coverage), and with t(df = 1) they were about 4x wider. The stated mechanism and direction are wrong in the main case.

citations.cite: Wolter KM. Introduction to Variance Estimation, 2nd ed. Springer 2007 (ignoring stratification is conservative under the with-replacement approximation)
Lumley T. Complex Surveys: A Guide to Analysis Using R. Wiley 2010 (nest=TRUE for PSU codes reused within strata)

bite_note: The refusal holds up the answer, and the warning tells the researcher their intervals are anticonservative when, with correctly coded PSUs, they are conservative. The gate is justified only by the reused-PSU-code hazard, which the claim does not name.

failing_part: "marks a near dependency among the exposure and adjustment set ... which of the dependent columns are held fixed changes what the exposure's estimate means" (with the intercept included and columns uncentered)
narrowest_regime: Holds for near dependencies among substantive columns that reflect a composition or near-sum constraint (e.g., nutrients and total energy, time-use parts), where holding the partners fixed forces a substitution. The 30 / 0.5 thresholds are BKW's detection conventions.
reason: With the intercept kept and columns scaled but not centered, as BKW recommend, an exposure with a small coefficient of variation forms a near dependency with the constant. In a check, height in cm (170 +/- 10) with independent sex and smoking gave CI 43 with VDP 1.0 on both the intercept and height; age 55-65 gave CI 47. Under the rule these become an 'act on it' adjustment-set decision, yet there is no adjustment partner to choose and nothing in the estimand changes. More generally, BKW's diagnostics measure how precisely coefficients are estimated. Whether holding a partner fixed changes the exposure's meaning is true of any adjustment, collinear or not. The 'less of what it replaces' reading needs a compositional dependency, which the diagnostic does not identify.

citations.cite: Belsley DA, Kuh E, Welsch RE. Regression Diagnostics: Identifying Influential Data and Sources of Collinearity. Wiley 1980, ch. 3 (CI >= 30, VDP > 0.5)
Belsley DA. Demeaning conditioning diagnostics through centering. Am Stat 1984;38:73-77 (intercept-involved dependencies under uncentered scaling)

bite_note: Exposures in natural units with large means (height in cm, age in a narrow band, year, BMI) would raise a spurious 'changes the question' Decide at the adjustment question, sending researchers to rethink an adjustment set that has no collinearity problem.

failing_part: "below 0.3 no such noticing is raised" (making the substitution-vs-addition question depend on |r(exposure, energy)| >= 0.3)
narrowest_regime: The first half holds at every correlation: the energy model always changes what the coefficient means. A correlation threshold can at most say how far the crude (energy-unadjusted) estimate is from the adjusted one, and even that also depends on energy's own effect. There is no regime where r alone settles whether the question changes.
reason: If Y = b1*N + b2*(E - N), the coefficient on N holding E fixed (substitution) is b1 - b2, while holding other energy fixed (addition) gives b1. The gap is b2, the effect of the energy the nutrient displaces, and corr(N, E) plays no part in it. In a simulation with corr(N, E) = 0.14, below the threshold, the substitution estimate was -0.22 and the addition estimate +0.18 per 100 kcal, opposite signs. The 0.3 cut-off is backed only by internal documents, and I know of no literature that ties the meaning of energy-adjustment models to an r threshold (Willett et al. 1997 and Tomova et al. 2022 frame the choice as an estimand question).

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Arnold KF, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Adjustment for energy intake in nutritional research: a causal inference perspective. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;115:189-198
Tomova GD, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects in nutritional epidemiology. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;116:1379-1388
Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S

bite_note: For a nutrient weakly correlated with energy (|r| < 0.3), the app suppresses the energy-model decision, but substitution and addition estimates can still differ in size or even sign. The researcher then reports one estimand without being told it is a choice.

narrowest_regime: Dietary substitution models where a constant kcal-per-unit factor would be applied. One caveat: 'lb' is a mass unit and could in principle record a food amount (lb of meat/week), in which case a kcal factor exists; as a body-measure unit it is correctly refused.
reason: One percentage point of energy equals 0.01 x E kcal, so its kcal content varies by person with total energy and there is no constant factor. In nutrient-density models, substitutions are properly expressed as percentage points of energy exchanged, with total energy held fixed (e.g., replacing 5% of energy from saturated fat with PUFA). Columns measuring height, age or body weight are not food quantities, so a kcal-per-unit substitution through them is meaningless and refusing it is correct.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S (nutrient density model)

bite_note: Without the refusal, applying a fixed kcal factor to a %-energy column would misstate the substitution contrast, since the true kcal swap differs with each person's total energy.

narrowest_regime: Regression outcomes scored by squared error, where each held-out row's baseline is the mean of the rows its model was trained on (that fold's training mean under CV).
reason: An out-of-sample R^2 compares the model with the null predictor actually available at prediction time, which is the training mean, and pooling squared errors over all out-of-fold predictions before forming the ratio avoids the bias and instability of averaging per-fold R^2. This is the definition and estimator Hawinkel, Waegeman & Maere give (null model 'uses the average outcome of the observed data'; losses 'summed over all observations before combining them into the final R^2'). Using test-fold means instead, as sklearn's r2_score does per fold, slightly flatters the model.

citations.cite: Hawinkel S, Waegeman W, Maere S. Out-of-sample R^2: estimation and inference. Am Stat 2024;78(1):15-25 (arXiv 2302.05131)

bite_note: Against pooled R^2 with the test mean, the difference is O(1/n) and negligible at realistic n. It matters only for small n with small test folds, where fold-averaged R^2 is noticeably biased.

failing_part: "decides how the rows are validated ... not the model's intercepts, so fixed-effects ... adjustment is refused"
narrowest_regime: When the model will be applied to new groups (new sites or participants not in the data), group-specific fixed intercepts cannot be used for prediction, and a cluster-robust SE alone changes nothing about the predictions. There, grouped folds and internal-external validation are the right response and refusing those two options is sound.
reason: The validation half is correct: grouped CV and internal-external validation across sites are the recommended practice (Steyerberg & Harrell 2016; Debray et al. 2013). But the literature also says the grouping should inform the model itself. Falconieri et al. (2020) found that conditional models, both random-intercept and fixed-effects logistic regression, gave calibrated within-center predictions when samples were large enough, while standard logistic regression was miscalibrated; they recommend random-intercept LR, which calibrated better even in a new center. Bouwmeester et al. (2013) found better discrimination with random intercepts when cluster effects are used. So when predictions are for groups already in the data, center intercepts improve accuracy, and 'not the model's intercepts' is wrong as a general rule.

citations.cite: Steyerberg EW, Harrell FE Jr. Prediction models need appropriate internal, internal-external, and external validation. J Clin Epidemiol 2016;69:245-247
Debray TP et al. A framework for developing, implementing, and evaluating clinical prediction models in an individual participant data meta-analysis. Stat Med 2013;32:3158-3180

Falconieri N, Van Calster B, Timmerman D, Wynants L. Developing risk models for multicenter data using standard logistic regression produced suboptimal predictions: a simulation study. Biom J 2020;62:932-944
Bouwmeester W et al. Prediction models for clustered data: comparison of a random intercept and standard regression model. BMC Med Res Methodol 2013;13:19

bite_note: When the model will be used in the same sites or for the same participants, refusing group intercepts (fixed or random) gives worse within-group calibration and discrimination than a conditional model; the refusal costs nothing only when every target group is new.

failing_part: "chooses the number of trees well once the plan's effective size is at least 1,500 ... below 1,500, searching the number of trees directly is better"; also "about 100 or more units of the rarest class"
narrowest_regime: The arithmetic works only if 'effective size' counts rarest-class units: 1,500 x 0.8 x 0.8 (nested 5-fold) x 0.1 = 96. If it means total rows, a 10% stopping set inside an inner fit holds about 96-150 rows in total, and at most half of those (<= 75) belong to the rarest class.
reason: The claim offers no citation or experiment, only internal recipe rows, for the 1,500 cut-off, the 10% share, patience 20/50 or the conclusion that searching tree counts beats early stopping below it. Early stopping on a held-out set is standard (Friedman 2001; XGBoost/LightGBM practice), but where it starts to beat a CV search over n_trees depends on the learning rate, noise, outcome type and how flat the validation-loss curve is. No general n threshold is known to me, and none was shown. The '100 units of the rarest class' figure is consistent only under an unstated definition of effective size.

citations.cite: Friedman JH. Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine. Ann Stat 2001;29:1189-1232

bite_note: With shrinkage, validation loss is usually flat near the optimal number of trees, so early stopping versus a direct search typically changes held-out performance little. The setting mainly affects compute and the run-to-run variance of the chosen tree count.

failing_part: "interval must come from a bootstrap over the whole chain" (and the fixed '5 times' re-imputation presented as required)
narrowest_regime: The refusal half holds: model-based outcome-model SEs, and Rubin's rules over per-copy model-based variances, ignore calibration-parameter uncertainty and are too narrow. The gap is small only when the calibration sub-study is large relative to the main study. A whole-chain bootstrap that respects the design (and resamples the main and calibration samples or sub-study membership separately) is one valid route.
reason: The cited source contradicts 'must'. Keogh, Shaw & Gustafson §6.1.2 says model SEs 'will be too small' but that SEs 'may be obtained either from a bootstrap variance estimator or a sandwich estimator obtained by stacking the calibration and outcome model estimating equations', and favors the bootstrap only for 'ease of implementation'. Stacked estimating equations (Carroll et al. 2006, App. B) are an equally valid design-based alternative, and with survey designs they come straight from linearization. Under Boot-MI, the number of imputations per resample is a Monte Carlo/compute trade-off (Schomaker & Heumann 2018), not a methods requirement fixed at 5.

citations.cite: Keogh RH, Shaw PA, Gustafson P, et al. STRATOS guidance document on measurement error and misclassification of variables in observational epidemiology: Part 1. Stat Med 2020;39:2197-2231, §6.1.2 (quote checked)
Schomaker M, Heumann C. Bootstrap inference when using multiple imputation. Stat Med 2018;37:2252-2266
Carroll RJ, Ruppert D, Stefanski LA, Crainiceanu CM. Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models, 2nd ed. Chapman & Hall 2006, Appendix B (stacked estimating equations)
Rao JNK, Wu CFJ. Resampling inference with complex survey data. JASA 1988;83:231-241

bite_note: Refusing model-based intervals widens them, correctly, and can change significance. Insisting on the bootstrap alone changes little in large samples, since a stacked sandwich gives similar intervals, but it forbids a valid, cheaper and deterministic method, including where a design bootstrap with few PSUs per stratum is unstable.
